The Case for Accountability: Why Hillary Clinton Should Face Prosecution

Introduction

No republic can long endure if it maintains two systems of justice—one for ordinary citizens and another for the politically powerful. I. The Private Email Server: A Clear Violation of Federal Law

The most thoroughly documented case against Clinton involves her use of a private email server housed in her Chappaqua, New York residence while serving as Secretary of State from 2009 to 2013. The facts of this case are largely undisputed.

Clinton transmitted and received over 100 emails containing information that was classified at the time it was sent, including emails at the Top Secret/Special Access Program level—the most sensitive category of national security information the United States government maintains. Under 18 U.S.C. § 793(f), the grossly negligent handling of national defense information is a federal crime. The statute does not require intent; negligence alone satisfies the legal standard.

Yet when FBI Director James Comey delivered his now-infamous July 2016 statement, he introduced a standard that exists nowhere in the statute—"intent." While describing Clinton's behavior as "extremely careless," Comey declined to recommend prosecution, effectively rewriting federal law from a podium. Legal scholars across the political spectrum noted the irregularity. Former Attorney General Michael Mukasey, federal prosecutor Andrew McCarthy, and numerous other legal authorities observed that the statute plainly criminalizes gross negligence, and that "extremely careless" is functionally indistinguishable from "grossly negligent."

Consider the contrast with other cases. Naval reservist Bryan Nishimura was convicted in 2015 for storing classified materials on personal devices—without any evidence of intent to distribute them and without evidence that hostile actors accessed them. Petty Officer First Class Kristian Saucier served a year in federal prison for taking photographs inside a nuclear submarine. Neither Nishimura nor Saucier held a position remotely comparable to Secretary of State, and neither handled information at the SAP level.

The disparity is not subtle. It is a canyon. If Saucier deserved imprisonment, then the standard, applied equally, demands that Clinton face prosecution for conduct that was orders of magnitude more serious in scope, volume, and potential damage to national security.

Her staff physically destroyed mobile devices with hammers. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 and 18 U.S.C. § 2071, the destruction of records under subpoena and the concealment of government documents are federal felonies. These are not ambiguous accusations—they are documented actions that Clinton's own representatives acknowledged.

II. The Clinton Foundation: Pay-to-Play at the Highest Level

The Clinton Foundation and its various initiatives operated during Hillary Clinton's tenure as Secretary of State in a manner that by any reasonable interpretation constituted a conflict of interest and, arguably, public corruption.

During Clinton's time at the State Department, the Foundation received tens of millions of dollars from foreign governments, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, and other nations that had direct business before the Secretary of State. A 2016 Associated Press investigation found that more than half of the private citizens who obtained meetings with Secretary Clinton had donated to the Clinton Foundation. This was not coincidence—it was a pattern so consistent that it constituted a system.

The Uranium One transaction is particularly illustrative. Between 2009 and 2013, the Russian state nuclear agency Rosatom acquired a controlling stake in Uranium One, a company that held rights to approximately 20 percent of U.S. uranium production capacity. The deal required approval from the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), on which the State Department held a seat. During and around this period, individuals connected to the Uranium One deal donated approximately $145 million to the Clinton Foundation. Clinton defenders argue that she did not personally approve the deal and that multiple agencies were involved. This defense is technically accurate but deliberately narrow. The question is not whether Clinton single-handedly approved the transaction but whether the pattern of donations created an environment of expected reciprocity—whether, in effect, foreign interests were purchasing access to and favorable treatment from the U.S. government through donations to the Clinton family's philanthropic apparatus.

Under 18 U.S.C. § 201 (bribery of public officials), the critical legal question is whether something of value was given to a public official with the intent to influence official acts. The circumstantial evidence—the volume, the timing, the consistency of the pattern—is precisely the kind of evidence prosecutors routinely use to secure corruption convictions against state and local officials. The only reason it has not been used here is the political stature of the accused.

III. Benghazi and the Culture of Deception

While the September 11, 2012 attack on the U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya may not in itself constitute a prosecutable criminal offense, the response to it reveals the culture of deception that has characterized Clinton's career and that compounds the case for accountability.

Four Americans—Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens, Sean Smith, Tyrone Woods, and Glen Doherty—died in the attack. When Clinton later told a congressional committee, "What difference, at this point, does it make?" she revealed an attitude toward accountability that is fundamentally incompatible with public trust. IV. Obstruction and Institutional Corruption

Perhaps the most troubling dimension of the Clinton case is the evidence that institutions meant to enforce the law were themselves compromised in ways that shielded her from accountability.

These are not conspiracy theories. They are documented facts established through inspector general investigations and congressional inquiries. They paint a picture of an investigation that was managed to reach a predetermined conclusion—not an investigation conducted to determine the truth and apply the law equally.

V. The Principle at Stake

The argument for prosecuting and, upon conviction, imprisoning Hillary Clinton ultimately rests not on partisan animus but on a foundational principle: the law must apply equally to all citizens, regardless of political power, social status, or institutional connections.

Thomas Paine wrote that "in America, the law is king." John Adams enshrined in the Massachusetts Constitution the ideal of "a government of laws, and not of men." These are not antiquated platitudes—they are the operating principles without which democratic self-governance becomes impossible.

When ordinary Americans see a naval reservist imprisoned for mishandling classified material while a Secretary of State walks free after doing the same thing on a vastly larger scale, they draw the rational conclusion that the system is rigged. When they see a foundation receiving hundreds of millions from foreign governments while its namesake makes decisions affecting those same governments, and no investigation follows, they lose faith in institutional integrity. When they see evidence destroyed under subpoena with no consequence, they conclude that the rules apply only to those without power.

This erosion of trust is not abstract. It manifests in declining institutional confidence, increasing political radicalization, and a pervasive cynicism that poisons democratic participation. Every day that passes without accountability reinforces the message that power insulates against consequence.

Critics will argue that prosecuting Clinton would be "political persecution" or "criminalizing political disagreement." This objection inverts reality. The politicization occurred when Clinton received treatment unavailable to any other citizen. Prosecution would not be the introduction of politics into law—it would be the removal of politics from law. Applying the same statutes to Clinton that are applied to military personnel and government employees is not persecution; it is equality.

Others will argue that prosecution would be "divisive." This argument, taken to its logical conclusion, would mean that no sufficiently prominent person could ever be prosecuted because doing so would upset their supporters. It is an argument for aristocratic immunity dressed in the language of social harmony. A nation that cannot prosecute the powerful is not avoiding division—it is institutionalizing injustice.

Some will point to the passage of time. But there is no statute of limitations on the principle of equal justice, and many of the relevant statutes carry limitations periods that, given the ongoing nature of concealment and obstruction, may not have fully run.

The case for prosecuting Hillary Clinton is not rooted in political vendetta. It is rooted in evidence, in law, and in the principle that a republic that exempts the powerful from accountability has ceased to function as a republic. The private email server, the destruction of subpoenaed evidence, the intertwining of Foundation donations with State Department access, and the institutional corruption that shielded all of it from consequence—these constitute a pattern that the justice system is designed to address.

Imprisonment, upon conviction through due process, would not be an act of political revenge. It would be a declaration that the United States still operates under the rule of law. It would be a message to every future officeholder that public service is a trust, not a license. And it would begin to repair the damage that years of visible, unanswered corruption have inflicted upon the public's faith in its own institutions.

The question is not whether we can afford to hold Hillary Clinton accountable. The question is whether we can afford not to.
